generic.text:
A worthy addition to the
collection. Hoo!

examine_fish.text:
Hoo! A fine fish. We shall keep
it in excellent care — no, I
shan't be eating it. Off it goes
to the tanks.

examine_bug.text:
Yes. An insect. Quite. I'll pop
it in a case at arm's length and
try not to look at it too
closely.

examine_fossil.text:
Hoo! A genuine fossil, and a
lovely specimen. The past made
solid. I could study it for
hours.

examine_art.text:
Hoo my. A real work of art. We
are honoured to give it a wall
of its own.

fossil_0.text:
The horned face itself.
Triceratops carried three horns
and a great bony frill — armour
against far worse company.

fossil_1.text:
The tail of Triceratops. Short
and stiff, nothing like the
whip-tails of the long-necks.
Balance, mostly.

fossil_2.text:
The body of Triceratops. A four-
legged plant-eater the size of
an elephant, and rather harder
to argue with.

fossil_3.text:
The skull of Tyrannosaurus.
Those jaws could crush bone
outright. I confess a small
thrill of terror. Hoo!

fossil_4.text:
The tail of Tyrannosaurus. Thick
and muscular — it
counterweighted that enormous
head as the beast ran.

fossil_5.text:
The body of Tyrannosaurus.
Barrel-chested, bird-hipped, and
standing on two tremendous legs.
Magnificent.

fossil_6.text:
The little head of Apatosaurus,
perched at the end of a very
great deal of neck. The brain
was famously modest.

fossil_7.text:
The tail of Apatosaurus — long,
tapering, and quite possibly
cracked like a whip to warn off
predators.

fossil_8.text:
The body of Apatosaurus. A long-
necked giant of the late
Jurassic; some grew past seventy
feet, nose to tail.

fossil_9.text:
The head of Stegosaurus. Tiny,
low-slung, and housing a brain
no larger than a walnut. And yet
it managed.

fossil_10.text:
The tail of Stegosaurus, tipped
with four fearsome spikes.
Palaeontologists call that
arrangement a thagomizer.

fossil_11.text:
The body of Stegosaurus, lined
with those famous kite-shaped
plates. Display, temperature, or
both — we still debate it.

fossil_12.text:
The skull of Pteranodon. A
toothless beak and a long
backward crest. Not a dinosaur
at all, but a flying reptile.

fossil_13.text:
The right wing of Pteranodon.
The wing was a membrane
stretched along one vastly
elongated finger. Elegant
engineering.

fossil_14.text:
The left wing of Pteranodon. A
span of over twenty feet, built
for gliding on sea winds after
fish.

fossil_15.text:
The head of a plesiosaur —
small, on a neck of astonishing
length. It ruled the Mesozoic
seas, not the land.

fossil_16.text:
The neck of the plesiosaur. Some
kinds carried forty and more
vertebrae in it. Imagine the
cricks.

fossil_17.text:
The body of the plesiosaur.
Broad, barrel-shaped, and driven
through the water by four great
flippers.

fossil_18.text:
The skull of a mammoth, tusks
and all. A cousin of today's
elephants, and a creature of the
Ice Age.

fossil_19.text:
The body of a mammoth. Woolly,
humped at the shoulder, and gone
only some ten thousand years
ago.

fossil_20.text:
Amber — fossil tree resin. Now
and then it traps an insect
whole, a small drama sealed for
millions of years.

fossil_21.text:
Petrified wood. The timber's
every cell has been replaced by
mineral, grain for grain. A tree
turned to stone.

fossil_22.text:
An ammonite. Not a snail but a
relative of the octopus, sealed
in a coiled shell. They died out
with the dinosaurs.

fossil_23.text:
A fossilised egg. I cannot say
whose. But picture the moment of
hatching — a whole life folded
inside the shell.

fossil_24.text:
A trilobite. A hard-shelled sea
creature from long before the
dinosaurs; there were thousands
upon thousands of kinds.

set_0.text:
That completes our Triceratops!
Hoo, what a day. A member of the
horned dinosaurs, it flourished
at the very end of the
Cretaceous — a three-horned
plant-eater the length of a bus,
with a solid neck frill for
defence. One of the last
dinosaurs standing before the
great extinction.

set_1.text:
Our Tyrannosaurus is complete! I
am quite beside myself. The
tyrant lizard was among the
largest land carnivores that
ever lived: a huge head, a short
muscular neck, and jaws set with
teeth the size of railway
spikes. Resistance, one
imagines, was rather futile.

set_2.text:
Apatosaurus, complete at last! A
diplodocid — one of the long-
necked sauropods of the late
Jurassic. You may know it as
brontosaurus. It reached some
seventy feet, with a small head,
a great column of a neck, and a
whip of a tail.

set_3.text:
The Stegosaurus is finished! A
plated dinosaur of the late
Jurassic, famous for the double
row of bony plates along its
back and the four spikes on its
tail. Formidable at one end; not
terribly bright at the other.

set_4.text:
Our Pteranodon is complete! Not
a dinosaur but a flying reptile
that lived among them. With a
wingspan past twenty feet it
soared on sea winds rather than
flapping, scooping fish in its
long toothless beak.

set_5.text:
The plesiosaur is assembled! An
aquatic reptile of the Mesozoic
seas — broad-bodied, four-
flippered, some with long necks
and small heads, others the
reverse. The first one was
described back in 1824.

set_6.text:
The mammoth stands complete! A
mammal, and a far more recent
one than the dinosaurs — a
creature of the Ice Age that
died out only about ten thousand
years ago, right as humankind
was spreading. Food for thought,
that.

collection_complete.text:
Wait — is it... yes! An entire
collection, complete! Huzzah! I
could molt with joy. Splendid
work, truly.

museum_complete.text:
Hoo! HOO, I say! Every wing
full, every collection finished.
A museum to stand beside the
finest in the world — and built
entirely by this town. I am
simply erupting with pride.

fish_crucian_carp.text:
A humble crucian carp. Common,
yes, but every thread matters in
the great tapestry. We'll mind
it well.

fish_brook_trout.text:
A brook trout, from cool, clean,
fast water. Where you find one,
the stream itself is in good
health.

fish_carp.text:
A carp — hardy, long-lived, and
quite happy in murky water that
would see other fish off.
Admirable, in its way.

fish_koi.text:
A koi. An ornamental carp,
really, bred over centuries for
colour. Catching one feels oddly
like landing a small fortune.

fish_catfish.text:
A catfish. Those barbels are not
whiskers but taste organs — it
can taste the water all around
itself. Remarkable.

fish_small_bass.text:
A young black bass. It will grow
into a proper predator; for now
it is all appetite and ambition.

fish_bass.text:
A black bass. An ambush hunter
that lurks by weed and timber
and strikes at anything smaller
than itself.

fish_large_bass.text:
A large black bass — a real
prize. Anglers travel a long way
for a fish this size. We're glad
it came to us.

fish_bluegill.text:
A bluegill. A small sunfish that
guards its nest fiercely against
all comers, whatever the size
difference.

fish_giant_catfish.text:
A giant catfish! These monsters
keep to the deeper ponds. I'll
watch over this one myself, hoo.

fish_giant_snakehead.text:
A giant snakehead. A fierce
thing that can gulp air and even
wriggle overland between pools.
Do cook it thoroughly.

fish_barbel_steed.text:
A barbel steed. A schooling
river fish that grubs along the
bottom with its downturned
mouth. Tidy little creature.

fish_dace.text:
A dace. A quick, silvery fish of
running water, forever darting
after insects at the surface.

fish_pale_chub.text:
A pale chub. Small, bright, and
bold — it will rise to almost
any fly. Beginners' luck, made
fish.

fish_bitterling.text:
A bitterling. It lays its eggs
inside a living freshwater
mussel, which carries them to
safety. An odd arrangement, but
it works.

fish_loach.text:
A loach. A bottom-dweller that
can breathe through its gut when
the water turns foul. Nature is
nothing if not inventive.

fish_pond_smelt.text:
A pond smelt. A cold-weather
fish, fished through the ice in
winter. It has a faint scent of
cucumber, they say.

fish_sweetfish.text:
A sweetfish. It appears as the
days grow long and is treated as
summer's herald — then promptly
eaten. Poor dear.

fish_cherry_salmon.text:
A cherry salmon. Some run to the
sea and return; others spend
their whole lives in the
mountain streams.

fish_large_char.text:
A large char. A char of the cold
headwaters, and a fine one. It
will want for nothing here.

fish_rainbow_trout.text:
A rainbow trout. Named for the
band of colour along its flank.
A strong swimmer that loves
broken water.

fish_stringfish.text:
A stringfish! Hoo, indeed — a
rare giant of the winter rivers.
We have been saving a place for
this very fish.

fish_salmon.text:
A salmon, returned from the sea
to the river of its birth to
spawn. A journey of
extraordinary determination.

fish_goldfish.text:
A goldfish. Bred from a plain
carp over a thousand years and
more. Proof of what patience can
do.

fish_piranha.text:
A piranha. Fewer teeth in its
reputation than in the water,
thankfully — but I shall handle
it with respect.

fish_arowana.text:
An arowana. It cruises just
under the surface and can leap
clear to snatch insects from low
branches.

fish_eel.text:
An eel. It breeds far out in the
ocean and no one has ever truly
watched it happen. A genuine
mystery, still.

fish_freshwater_goby.text:
A freshwater goby. Its pelvic
fins are fused into a little
suction cup, so it can hold
station in a current.

fish_angelfish.text:
An angelfish. Tall, banded, and
serene — though rather
territorial once it decides a
corner is home.

fish_guppy.text:
A guppy. Small, gaudy, and
astonishingly prolific. The
males wear all the colour; the
females do all the work.

fish_popeyed_goldfish.text:
A popeyed goldfish. Those
enormous eyes are a bred trait,
not a wild one. Charming, if a
touch alarming.

fish_coelacanth.text:
A coelacanth! Hoo my. A fish
thought extinct for millions of
years until one turned up in a
net. A living fossil.

fish_crawfish.text:
A crawfish — a crayfish, really,
a small freshwater cousin of the
lobster. Those pincers are
stronger than they look.

fish_frog.text:
A frog. Not a fish at all, of
course, but we keep amphibians
too. It shall have all the damp
comforts of home.

fish_killifish.text:
A killifish. A tiny thing of
ricefields and ditches that
survives where almost nothing
else will.

fish_jellyfish.text:
A jellyfish. Ninety-odd percent
water, no brain, no heart, and
drifting the seas since long
before us. Beautiful, at a
distance.

fish_sea_bass.text:
A sea bass. It changes its
haunts with the seasons, moving
between deep water and the
shallows. We'll settle it in.

fish_red_snapper.text:
A red snapper. A handsome, deep-
bodied sea fish, long considered
a fish for celebrations.

fish_barred_knifejaw.text:
A barred knifejaw. Its beak-like
teeth are fused for crushing
shellfish and barnacles clean
off the rocks.

fish_arapaima.text:
An arapaima! One of the largest
freshwater fish in the world,
and an air-breather besides. A
tremendous catch.

bug_ant.text:
An ant. Industrious, I grant
you. Also everywhere, and given
to swarming anything sweet. I'll
seal the case now.

bug_bagworm.text:
A bagworm — a moth caterpillar
in a case of stitched leaves. It
can strip a tree bare. Wretched
appetite.

bug_banded_dragonfly.text:
A banded dragonfly. A superb
flier, I'll admit. I simply wish
it would do its superb flying
elsewhere.

bug_bee.text:
A bee. It takes some nerve to
bring one of these here intact.
I trust you were stung only a
little. Blech.

bug_bell_cricket.text:
A bell cricket. The song is
genuinely lovely on an autumn
evening. The insect making it,
rather less so.

bug_brown_cicada.text:
A brown cicada. It spends years
underground and a fortnight
above it, most of that fortnight
shouting. Loudly.

bug_cockroach.text:
A... cockroach. I will never
understand why the regulations
require these. In it goes.
Quickly. Ugh.

bug_common_butterfly.text:
A common butterfly. Pretty
enough on the wing. Up close it
is all dust and twitching legs.
Hooo.

bug_common_dragonfly.text:
A common dragonfly. Two enormous
compound eyes that see almost
everything at once. Unsettling,
frankly.

bug_cricket.text:
A cricket. It sings by scraping
one wing against the other. A
whole orchestra of friction
under the grass.

bug_darner_dragonfly.text:
A darner dragonfly, one of the
larger sorts. It can hover, and
fly backwards. I'd rather it
didn't.

bug_drone_beetle.text:
A drone beetle. It flies with a
droning buzz, as advertised, and
blunders into everything.
Including me.

bug_dynastid_beetle.text:
A rhinoceros beetle. It can
shift many times its own weight
with that horn. Impressive. Also
enormous. Away it goes.

bug_evening_cicada.text:
An evening cicada. Its call at
dusk is genuinely mournful and
rather beautiful. I still won't
be touching it.

bug_firefly.text:
A firefly. It makes cold light
in its abdomen through pure
chemistry. Magical to watch.
Best from a distance.

bug_flat_stag_beetle.text:
A flat stag beetle. Those jaws
are for wrestling rival males
off the branch, not for me.
Small mercies.

bug_giant_beetle.text:
A giant beetle! Hoo. Yes. It is
certainly giant. That is rather
the whole problem. Into the
largest case.

bug_grasshopper.text:
A grasshopper. The hind legs
come away far too easily when
one handles it. I would rather
not dwell on that.

bug_jewel_beetle.text:
A jewel beetle. That iridescence
has been prized for ornament for
centuries. On the beetle, I find
it nauseating.

bug_ladybug.text:
A ladybug. I had hopes for this
one. Then I touched it, and it
wept a foul yellow fluid onto my
feathers. Never again.

bug_long_locust.text:
A long locust. Harmless alone.
In numbers it becomes a plague
that darkens the sky and strips
the fields.

bug_longhorn_beetle.text:
A longhorn beetle. The antennae
can be longer than the body.
Why? No one has ever given me a
satisfactory answer.

bug_mantis.text:
A mantis. It turns its head to
watch you, which no proper
insect should be able to do. I
find it deeply judgemental.

bug_migratory_locust.text:
A migratory locust. Crowd them
together and they change colour,
temperament, and destiny. Then
they eat everything.

bug_mole_cricket.text:
A mole cricket. It lives
underground and sings from down
there, so you hear it but never
see it. Small blessing.

bug_mosquito.text:
A mosquito. Only the females
bite, for the protein to lay
eggs. Knowing that has never
once stopped the itching.

bug_mountain_beetle.text:
A mountain beetle. Handsome, in
the way armoured things are
handsome. It still opens up into
flapping wings. No.

bug_pill_bug.text:
A pill bug. Not an insect but a
land crustacean. It rolls into a
ball when frightened. So,
frankly, do I.

bug_pine_cricket.text:
A pine cricket. Another fine
autumn singer. I do enjoy the
concert. I attend it strictly
from indoors.

bug_pond_skater.text:
A pond skater. It stands on the
surface film without breaking
it. An affront to the natural
order, if you ask me.

bug_purple_butterfly.text:
A purple butterfly. A rarer,
richer colour than the common
sort. Still made of dust and
legs, alas.

bug_red_dragonfly.text:
A red dragonfly. It reddens as
it matures, and gathers in great
crowds in autumn. Then it
gathers near me. Blech.

bug_robust_cicada.text:
A robust cicada — one of the
biggest and by far the loudest.
Its song is roughly the volume
of a passing train.

bug_saw_stag_beetle.text:
A saw stag beetle. The toothed
jaws give it the name. They are
for other beetles. I remind
myself of that firmly.

bug_snail.text:
A snail. A mollusc, not an
insect — a cousin of the oyster,
believe it or not. Soft, damp,
and dreadful to hold.

bug_spider.text:
A spider. Eight legs, eight
eyes, and an all-insect diet.
Useful, one supposes. I will
keep this glass between us.

bug_spotted_ladybug.text:
A spotted ladybug. More spots,
same foul trick when alarmed.
I've learned my lesson. Straight
into the case.

bug_tiger_butterfly.text:
A tiger butterfly, boldly
striped as a warning. On the
wing it is quite grand. I shall
admire it through the lid.

bug_walker_cicada.text:
A walker cicada. It calls in the
heat of high summer, on and on,
until the whole afternoon seems
made of noise.

bug_yellow_butterfly.text:
A yellow butterfly. It drifts
about the flowers looking like a
stray petal. Then it lands on
you. Hoo.
